processing: A way of serving tea: strong black tea, kept hot and diluted in the bowl with milk or cream. Kazakhs in Xinjiang, China, may start with a pinch of salt and fresh milk, and also make a flour tea, un shai.
harvest_season: Not applicable; it depends on the black tea used.
appearance_liquor: Typically a dark reddish brown before any milk is added.
appearance_wet: Dark brown leaf, as with other strong black teas.
taste_profile: Strong, malty black tea softened by milk or cream, with a brisk finish; some versions add fennel or cardamom, and a pinch of salt appears in Xinjiang Kazakh practice.

brewing.notes: A home approximation: brew a strong pot of black tea and serve it in small amounts with sweets. Households differ, and there is no single recipe.

vintage_note: It has no vintages or seasons, since this is a serving custom using ordinary black tea, bought as needed and drunk fresh.
description:
In Kazakhstan, tea is the drink that accompanies nearly every meal, and hosting people properly means keeping their bowls full. The usual cup is strong black tea with milk or cream, served in a ceramic bowl: small ones, called kese or piyala, in the hot south and west, larger ones elsewhere.

The name kyzyl shai, red tea, refers to the rich reddish colour of a strong brew with milk. Traditionally it is kept steeping on a hot stove. Kazakhs in Xinjiang, China, may start with a pinch of salt and fresh milk, and also make a flour tea called un shai.

In the cup it should be strong and malty, with enough milk to round it off and not hide it. Weak tea is the usual mistake: the milk needs something to stand up to. Fennel or cardamom are sometimes added, which gives a warm spiced version.

Accounts of how to pour disagree. Some describe a nearly full bowl as generous, others hold that a small pour is the respectful one, because the guest then gets refilled more often. It varies by region and family, so follow your host.

Serve it the way it comes at the table, with dried curd such as kurt and sweets on the dastarkhan.
history: Black tea reached the Kazakhs from China along the Silk Road trade routes, though no firm date is attached to this. It was traditionally taken with sweets after the main course. Today it accompanies every meal and has largely replaced other traditional drinks.
